sentences.text: Hyneria possessed a skull featuring heavy, ornamented dermal bones and a relatively long, shallow lower jaw.
The fish had stout teeth, including premaxillary fangs that were over 2 inches long.
Its body was covered in cycloid scales.
Large sensory canals helped the animal detect prey in the murky, low-visibility freshwater environments it inhabited.
This creature could measure up to two meters in length and weigh as much as half a ton.
Adult Hyneria retained juvenile skeletal features, suggesting they were likely neotenic.
Keith Thompson discovered fossilized teeth, bones, and a fin of Hyneria in the Red Hill Shale of Pennsylvania in 1968.
The genus name Hyneria refers to the village of Hyner in Pennsylvania, near the site of the first fossil discovery.
The species name H. lindae honors the wife of Keith Stewart Thomson, the scientist who first described the fish.
Despite many discoveries, a complete Hyneria skeleton has never been recovered.
Hyneria had powerful jaws and very sharp teeth, could swim very fast, and was a lethal predator.
Its ability to swim very fast made it a lethal predator.
The type species H. lindae is estimated to have reached a total length of 2.5 to 3 meters.
An isolated cleithrum suggests that some individuals of Hyneria were at least 2.7 meters long.
While the largest complete jaw is 38 cm, a larger fragment exists that might belong to a jaw twice that size, though it may actually be from a rhizodont.
If a large jaw fragment belongs to Hyneria, the animal could have reached lengths up to 3.5 meters.
The genus Hyneria was described by Thomson in 1968.
Hyneria belongs to the family Tristichopteridae.
Hyneria is classified within the superorder Osteolepidida.
Hyneria is a member of the class Sarcopterygii, known as lobe-finned fishes.
Hyneria was a large predatory lobe-finned fish that lived in freshwater during the Famennian stage of the Devonian period.
Hyneria fossils are found in the Catskill Formation of the Red Hill Shale, dating to the upper Devonian.
Hyneria lived during the Devonian period, approximately 360 million years ago.
Hyneria lived between 372.15 and 358.86 million years ago during the Famennian stage.
It is debated whether a large jaw fragment found in the area actually belongs to Hyneria or to a rhizodont.
